evidence.title: Present-day stellar constraints leave multiple high-energy histories for TOI-700 and LHS 1140
evidence.publisher: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
evidence.author: Zhang, Yuzhan
excerpts: Abstract Atmospheric evolution on temperate planets records integrated X-ray, extreme-ultraviolet (EUV) and stellar-wind forcing, whereas host stars are usually characterized from present-day measurements.
Rotation and activity histories can converge at late ages, leaving different cumulative exposures compatible with similar current states.
We quantify this inverse problem for TOI-700 and LHS 1140 without treating either planet as a calibrated atmospheric chronometer.
Among rotation-conditioned tracks, 194 histories matching TOI-700 span only a factor 1.077 in current EUV but factors 2.65 and 2.73 in cumulative EUV and wind exposure.
For LHS 1140, 97 rotation-matched histories span 1.0085 in current EUV but 1.567 and 1.543 cumulatively.
An independent X-ray measurement tests the present-activity mapping yet provides little ranking of these histories because their native current X-ray luminosities differ by only 0.0038 dex.

The results separate present-state admissibility, forward-model adequacy and historical identification, and show why an additional present observable need not reduce uncertainty in the historical forcing relevant to planetary evolution.

evidence.title: Explainable Machine Learning Prediction of Unknown Exoplanet Masses from Stellar and Orbital Parameters
evidence.author: Das, Swapan; Bhardwaj, Vinod  Kumar; Chakraborty, Janajit
excerpts: This study presents an explainable machine learning framework for predicting unknown exoplanet masses using stellar and orbital parameters obtained from the NASA Exoplanet Archive.

Following data preprocessing and feature selection, five ensemble regression algorithms—Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost—were developed and evaluated using an 80:20 train-test split and five-fold cross-validation.
Model performance was assessed using the coefficient of determination (R²), Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) and Mean Absolute Error (MAE).
Statistical differences among the models were examined using Friedman, Wilcoxon signed rank, and Nemenyi post-hoc tests.

Although XGBoost achieved the highest predictive accuracy on the independent test dataset (R² = 0.1281), Gradient Boosting demonstrated the strongest overall generalisation during cross-validation (R² = 0.2852) and was selected as the final prediction model.

To improve model interpretability, SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) were employed to quantify feature contributions, identifying the orbital period, planetary radius, stellar mass, system distance, and stellar surface gravity as the most influential predictors of planetary mass.
Furthermore, 95\% prediction intervals were generated to quantify the uncertainty for each estimated planetary mass.

The proposed framework provides an interpretable and statistically validated approach for estimating unknown exoplanet masses, together with prediction uncertainty estimates, to support future exoplanet characterisation and observational planning.

evidence.title: List of exoplanet extremes
excerpts: The following are lists of extremes among the known exoplanets.
The properties listed here are those for which values are known reliably.
The study of exoplanets is one of the most dynamic emerging fields of science, thus these values may change as new discoveries are made.

evidence.title: List of smallest known stars
excerpts: This is a list of the smallest known stars, brown dwarfs and stellar remnants, sorted by increasing size.

The list is divided into sublists, and contain notable objects up to 350,000 km in radius, or 0.50 R☉, as well as all red dwarfs smaller than 0.1 R☉ and all neutron stars with accurately measured radii.

evidence.title: TRAPPIST-1
excerpts: TRAPPIST-1 (also known as 2MASS J23062928−0502285 or SPECULOOS-1) is a red dwarf star with seven known exoplanets.
It lies in the constellation Aquarius approximately 40.66 light-years (12.47 pc) away from Earth.
An ultra-cool dwarf, it has a surface temperature of about 2,566 K (2,290 °C; 4,160 °F).
Its radius is slightly larger than Jupiter's and it has a mass of about 9% of the Sun.
It is estimated to be 7.6 billion years old, making it older than the Solar System.

Observations in 2016 from TRAPPIST–South (Transiting Planets and Planetesimals Small Telescope project) at La Silla Observatory in Chile and other telescopes led to the discovery of two terrestrial planets in orbit around TRAPPIST-1.
In 2017, further analysis of the original observations identified five more terrestrial planets.
The seven planets take between 1.5 and 19 days to orbit the star in circular orbits.
They are all likely tidally locked to TRAPPIST-1, and it is therefore believed that each planet is in permanent day on one side and permanent night on the other.
Their masses are comparable to that of Earth and they all lie in the same plane; seen from Earth, they pass in front of the star.
This placement allowed the planets to be detected: when they pass in front of the star, its apparent magnitude dims.
Up to four of the planets—designated d, e, f, and g—orbit at distances where temperatures are likely suitable for the existence of liquid water, and are thus potentially hospitable to life.
